etymology: Hebrew Shiloh (H7887), a town in the hill country of Ephraim; the name possibly means "place of rest" or "tranquillity." Distinct from the messianic title "Shiloh" of Genesis 49:10 (see the shiloh-doctrine entry).
biblical_def: Shiloh was the town in the hill country of Ephraim where the tabernacle of the LORD was set up after the conquest of Canaan, and which served as Israel's central place of worship for some three hundred years, through the period of the judges until the days of Samuel. After the land was subdued, "the whole congregation of the children of Israel assembled together at Shiloh, and set up the tabernacle of the congregation there" (Josh 18:1); there the remaining tribal allotments were divided by lot before the LORD. Shiloh became the seat of the ark and the worship of Israel through the era of the judges. It was at Shiloh that the barren Hannah prayed for a son and vowed him to the LORD, and there she brought the child Samuel to minister before Eli the priest (1 Sam 1-3). There the boy Samuel heard the voice of the LORD calling in the night. But Shiloh became also a place of judgment: under Eli's wicked sons Hophni and Phinehas, the worship was corrupted, and when Israel presumptuously carried the ark of Shiloh into battle against the Philistines, it was captured, Eli's sons were slain, and Eli died (1 Sam 4). The glory departed ("Ichabod"), and Shiloh's sanctuary was, it seems, destroyed. Centuries later the LORD pointed back to Shiloh's ruin as a solemn warning to those who trusted in the temple at Jerusalem: "Go ye now unto my place which was in Shiloh, where I set my name at the first, and see what I did to it for the wickedness of my people Israel" (Jer 7:12). Shiloh thus stands as a sobering monument: the place where God once set His name can be abandoned to ruin when His people corrupt His worship and presume upon His presence. Privilege without obedience is no security.
webster_summary: The town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood for some 300 years through the judges (Josh 18:1); where Hannah prayed, Samuel ministered, and the ark was lost under Eli's sons (1 Sam 1-4); later a warning of judgment on presumption (Jer 7:12).

corruption_summary: Shiloh the place is corrupted when confused with the messianic title Shiloh of Genesis 49:10, when its ruin is read as mere history rather than the warning Jeremiah makes it, or when the lesson of privilege-without-obedience is missed.
corruption_paragraphs: Place-and-title confusion. "Shiloh" in Scripture names two distinct things: the town in Ephraim where the tabernacle stood, and the messianic figure of Jacob's prophecy, "the sceptre shall not depart from Judah... until Shiloh come" (Gen 49:10), understood as a title of the Messiah (see the shiloh-doctrine entry). The two are unrelated in meaning and must not be conflated. This entry concerns the place; the messianic title is treated separately.

Ruin-as-mere-history misreading. The destruction of Shiloh's sanctuary can be read as a sad episode of Israel's early history and nothing more. Jeremiah reads it as a permanent warning: those in his day trusted in the temple at Jerusalem as a guarantee of God's protection regardless of their conduct ("The temple of the LORD, the temple of the LORD," Jer 7:4). The LORD points them to Shiloh's ruin: He had set His name there first, and He gave it to destruction for His people's wickedness. The lesson is sobering and permanent: the place where God sets His name is no security to a people who corrupt His worship and presume on His presence. Privilege without obedience invites the judgment that fell on Shiloh.

etymology: Hebrew Beth-El (H1008), "house of God," from bayit ("house") + El ("God"). A town north of Jerusalem in the hill country, originally called Luz, renamed by Jacob.
biblical_def: Bethel ("house of God") was one of the most significant places in the patriarchal and later history of Israel — a town north of Jerusalem where the LORD met Jacob, and which became, tragically, a center of idolatrous worship in the divided kingdom. The site first appears when Abraham pitched his tent and built an altar between Bethel and Ai (Gen 12:8). But it is chiefly associated with Jacob: fleeing from Esau, he slept there and saw the ladder reaching to heaven with the angels of God ascending and descending, and the LORD standing above it confirming the covenant promise. Jacob awoke and said, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not... this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven" (Gen 28:16-17); he named the place Bethel, "house of God" (it had been called Luz). Years later, the LORD called Jacob back to Bethel to build an altar and renew his vows (Gen 35:1-15). Bethel thus stands as a place of true encounter with God, where heaven touched earth and the covenant was confirmed — the very ladder the Lord Jesus would later apply to Himself as the true gate of heaven, the Mediator on whom the angels ascend and descend (John 1:51). Yet Bethel's later history is a tragic inversion: when the kingdom divided, Jeroboam I set up one of his two golden calves at Bethel (1 Kings 12:28-29), making the "house of God" a house of idols and a center of false worship for the northern kingdom. Amos and Hosea prophesied against it; the LORD called it not Bethel ("house of God") but Beth-aven ("house of vanity/iniquity," Hos 4:15). The good king Josiah later defiled and destroyed the altar there (2 Kings 23:15). Bethel's two histories — the gate of heaven and the house of idols — warn that the most sacred places can be corrupted, and that the name "house of God" is no protection where true worship is abandoned.
webster_summary: The town ("house of God") where Jacob saw the ladder to heaven and named the place (Gen 28); a true place of covenant encounter, prefiguring Christ the gate of heaven (John 1:51); later corrupted into a center of golden-calf worship by Jeroboam I (1 Kings 12:28-29).

corruption_summary: Bethel is corrupted when its glorious patriarchal history is severed from its later idolatry, when the ladder vision is missed as a type of Christ, or when the lesson that "house of God" can become "house of vanity" is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Ladder-typology missed. Jacob's vision at Bethel — the ladder set up on earth reaching to heaven, with the angels of God ascending and descending, and the LORD above it — is not merely a remarkable dream. The Lord Jesus applied it directly to Himself: "ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man" (John 1:51). Christ is the true ladder, the true Bethel, the one Mediator who joins heaven and earth, the gate of heaven through whom alone men come to God. To read the Bethel vision without seeing Christ is to miss the One the vision was given to reveal.

House-of-God-to-house-of-vanity warning. Bethel's tragedy is that the place named "house of God" (Beth-El) became, under Jeroboam, a house of idols, so that the prophet renamed it "Beth-aven" — house of vanity or iniquity (Hos 4:15; 5:8). The same site that had been the gate of heaven became a gate to false worship. The warning is permanent: a sacred name is no guarantee of sacred reality. Churches, denominations, and institutions that bear the name "house of God" can become houses of vanity when they abandon true worship for idols of their own making. Josiah's later destruction of Bethel's altar (2 Kings 23:15) shows that God will judge the corruption of His own house.

etymology: Hebrew Shekem (H7927), "shoulder, ridge" (from its position on the saddle between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim). A central town in the hill country of Ephraim. Distinct from Shechem the son of Hamor (Gen 34).
biblical_def: Shechem was a town of immense significance in the history of Israel, situated in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim in the hill country of Ephraim — a natural crossroads and a recurring site of covenant, worship, and decision. It was the first place in Canaan where Abraham stopped and built an altar, where the LORD appeared to him and promised the land to his seed (Gen 12:6-7). Jacob bought a parcel of ground there and built an altar (Gen 33:18-20); there he buried the foreign gods of his household under the oak (Gen 35:4); and there, later, the bones of Joseph were buried in the plot Jacob had bought (Josh 24:32). At Shechem, between Ebal and Gerizim, Joshua read the blessings and the curses of the Law to all Israel as the LORD had commanded (Josh 8:30-35), and there, at the end of his life, Joshua gathered all Israel for the great covenant renewal, setting before them the choice — "choose you this day whom ye will serve" — and declaring, "but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Josh 24:15). Shechem was later the place where the foolish Rehoboam went to be made king and, by his harshness, lost the ten tribes, so that the kingdom divided (1 Kings 12). In the New Testament, near Shechem (at Sychar, by Jacob's well and the plot of ground he gave Joseph) the Lord Jesus met the Samaritan woman and revealed Himself as the giver of living water and the one whom true worshippers must worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:5-26). Shechem thus runs like a thread through the whole biblical story — the place of Abraham's first altar, Jacob's worship, Joseph's burial, Joshua's covenant, the kingdom's division, and the Lord's revelation to a Samaritan sinner — a recurring place of covenant and decision before God.
webster_summary: A central town between Ebal and Gerizim; Abraham's first altar (Gen 12:6-7); Jacob's worship and Joseph's burial (Josh 24:32); Joshua's great covenant renewal, "choose you this day" (Josh 24:15); the kingdom's division (1 Kings 12); and near it (Sychar) the Lord met the Samaritan woman (John 4).

corruption_summary: Shechem is corrupted when its many-layered covenant history is flattened into a mere geographical note, when Joshua's covenant-renewal call is severed from its decisive demand, or when the Lord's meeting at the nearby well is read apart from the place's covenant significance.
corruption_paragraphs: Covenant-thread flattened. Shechem is not merely one more town on the map; it is a place to which the LORD returns His people again and again for covenant and decision: Abraham's first altar and first promise, Jacob's worship and burial of idols, Joseph's bones laid to rest, Joshua's reading of blessing and curse and his great covenant renewal, and at last the Lord Jesus's self-revelation at the nearby well. To read these as scattered, unconnected episodes is to miss the thread: Shechem is the recurring place where God meets His people and sets before them the choice to serve Him. The whole biblical story passes through Shechem.

Shechem has no significant postmodern redefinition as a place. The principal point worth recovering is the recurring demand for decision that the place embodies. At Shechem Joshua set the choice before all Israel: "choose you this day whom ye will serve" (Josh 24:15). At the nearby well the Lord set living water before a Samaritan sinner. The place of covenant is the place of decision: every generation must, like Joshua, choose whom it will serve, and declare with him, "as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."

etymology: Hebrew Chevron (H2275), possibly "association, league, confederacy" (from chavar, "to join"); anciently also called Kirjath-arba ("city of Arba"). A town in the hill country of Judah, among the oldest in the world.
biblical_def: Hebron was an ancient city in the hill country of Judah, deeply bound up with the patriarchs and with King David. Abraham dwelt by the oaks (plain) of Mamre at Hebron, where he built an altar (Gen 13:18) and where the LORD appeared to him and announced the birth of Isaac (Gen 18). When Sarah died at Hebron, Abraham purchased the cave of Machpelah there from Ephron the Hittite as a burial place (Gen 23) — the first piece of the promised land that the patriarchs owned, and the tomb in which Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah were all buried (Gen 49:31; 50:13). Thus Hebron holds the bones of the patriarchs, the down-payment of the land-promise. In the conquest, Hebron was given to Caleb, who at eighty-five drove out the giants (the sons of Anak) and took it as his inheritance, the reward of his wholehearted following of the LORD (Josh 14:6-15). It became one of the cities of refuge and a Levitical city (Josh 20:7; 21:11). Most notably, Hebron was David's first capital: there he was anointed king over Judah, and there he reigned seven and a half years before capturing Jerusalem and reigning over all Israel (2 Sam 2:1-4; 5:1-5). It was also at Hebron that Absalom raised the standard of his rebellion (2 Sam 15:7-10). Hebron thus links the patriarchs (in the tomb of Machpelah) to the Davidic kingdom (in David's first throne) — a place of burial, of inheritance won by faith (Caleb), and of the beginning of the kingdom from which the Son of David would come.

corruption_summary: Hebron is corrupted only when its dense patriarchal and Davidic significance is flattened, when the tomb of Machpelah is read as mere antiquity rather than the down-payment of the land-promise, or when Caleb's wholehearted faith that won Hebron is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Down-payment-of-promise missed. The cave of Machpelah at Hebron was the first piece of the promised land the patriarchs actually owned — Abraham bought it, in full and public transaction, as a burial place. There he laid Sarah, and there were laid Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah. The detail is theologically weighty: the patriarchs died in faith, not having received the promises, but the tomb of Machpelah was the pledge that the land would be theirs (Heb 11:13). They were buried in the land of promise as a down-payment of the inheritance their seed would possess. To read Machpelah as mere antiquity is to miss the faith that bought a grave as a claim on God's promise.

Hebron has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are the faith of the patriarchs who bought a burial-place as a pledge of the promise, and the wholehearted faith of Caleb who at eighty-five drove out the giants to claim Hebron as his inheritance — "because that he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel" (Josh 14:14). Hebron is a place won and held by faith, and the first throne of the Davidic kingdom from which the Son of David would come.

etymology: Hebrew Gibe'ah (H1390), "hill, height" (from geva, "hill"). A town in the territory of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem; "Gibeah of Saul," the hometown and royal seat of King Saul.
biblical_def: Gibeah was a town in the tribal territory of Benjamin, infamous as the scene of one of the darkest episodes in the book of Judges and later notable as the hometown and capital of King Saul. The dark episode comes at the end of Judges, in the days when "there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). A Levite and his concubine, traveling, lodged at Gibeah; the wicked men of the city surrounded the house and, in an outrage echoing the sin of Sodom, abused the concubine through the night until she died (Judg 19). The Levite's gruesome summons to the tribes provoked a civil war in which the tribe of Benjamin, defending the men of Gibeah, was nearly annihilated (Judg 20). Gibeah thus stands as a monument to the moral chaos of the period of the judges — what Israel became when every man did what was right in his own eyes, when even the covenant people sank to the depravity of Sodom. Later, Gibeah became the hometown and royal residence of Saul, the first king of Israel (1 Sam 10:26; 11:4; "Gibeah of Saul," 1 Sam 15:34), so that the town's name is bound to the tragic king whose reign began in promise and ended in rejection. The prophet Hosea later recalled Gibeah's ancient wickedness as a byword for the depth of Israel's corruption: "they have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah" (Hos 9:9; 10:9). Gibeah is a sober place: it testifies to how far a covenant people can fall when they cast off the fear of God, and it reminds the reader that the human heart, left to itself, is capable of Sodom's sins even within the visible people of God.

corruption_summary: Gibeah is corrupted when its horror is read as mere ancient barbarism rather than a mirror of the human heart, when the "every man did right in his own eyes" refrain is missed, or when the depravity within the covenant people is explained away.
corruption_paragraphs: Distant-barbarism dismissal. The outrage at Gibeah is so horrifying that modern readers may distance themselves from it as the barbarism of a primitive age, far removed from civilized people. The book of Judges intends the opposite effect: Gibeah was not a pagan city but a town of the covenant people Israel, and its men sank to the very sin of Sodom. The refrain that frames the episode — "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25) — is the diagnosis: when the fear of God is cast off and each person becomes his own law, even God's own people are capable of Sodom's depravity. Gibeah is a mirror, not a museum piece: it shows what the human heart, including the religious heart, becomes when it throws off God's law.

Gibeah has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is its testimony to the depth of human depravity even within the visible people of God, and the chaos that results when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 21:25). Our own age, which exalts the autonomy of the individual will and the right of each person to define right and wrong for himself, is the days of Gibeah in modern dress. The remedy then and now is the same: the King, the fear of God, and the rule of His Word over the autonomous self.

etymology: Hebrew Machanayim (H4266), "two camps" or "two hosts," the dual form of machaneh ("camp"). A town east of the Jordan in Gilead, named by Jacob.
biblical_def: Mahanaim ("two camps") was a town east of the Jordan in Gilead, named by Jacob at a moment of fear and divine assurance, and later a place of refuge for King David. Jacob named it on his return from Padan-aram, as he came back toward the land and toward his dreaded reckoning with Esau: "And Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him. And when Jacob saw them, he said, This is God's host: and he called the name of that place Mahanaim" (Gen 32:1-2). The two camps may refer to the camp of Jacob and the camp of the angelic host, or to the angelic host itself encamped about him; either way, the name testifies that as Jacob went fearfully to meet Esau, the LORD gave him the assurance of the unseen angelic army encamped around him (cf. 2 Kings 6:17, where Elisha's servant sees the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire). It was the visible reminder of the invisible truth that "the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them" (Ps 34:7). Centuries later, Mahanaim served as a place of refuge and safety in Israel's history: it was the capital from which Ish-bosheth, Saul's son, briefly reigned (2 Sam 2:8-9), and most notably it was the city to which David fled during Absalom's rebellion, where he was sheltered and supplied by faithful men (Barzillai and others) and from which his forces went out to the battle in which Absalom died (2 Sam 17:24-29; 18). Mahanaim thus carries a consistent significance: the place where God's people, in fear and flight, found that they were not alone — that the unseen host of God encamps around those who fear Him, and that the LORD provides refuge and help in the day of trouble.
webster_summary: A town in Gilead ("two camps") named by Jacob when the angels of God met him as he feared Esau (Gen 32:1-2), testifying to the unseen angelic host that encamps around those who fear God (Ps 34:7); later David's refuge during Absalom's rebellion (2 Sam 17).

corruption_summary: Mahanaim is corrupted only when its testimony to the unseen angelic host is missed, when the assurance it gave fearful Jacob and fleeing David is severed from the believer's comfort, or when it is read as a bare place-name.
corruption_paragraphs: Unseen-host missed. Mahanaim, "two camps," was named at the moment the angels of God met the fearful Jacob — a visible token of the invisible truth that God's host was encamped around His servant. The same truth is dramatized when Elisha's servant, terrified by the surrounding Syrian army, has his eyes opened to see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kings 6:17), and it is promised to all who fear God: "the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him" (Ps 34:7). Mahanaim is a standing comfort to the believer in fear and flight: he is not alone; the unseen camp of God surrounds him. To read Mahanaim as a bare place-name is to miss the comfort God built into its very name.

Mahanaim has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is its testimony to the unseen protection of God's people. As Jacob feared Esau and David fled Absalom, Mahanaim was the place where each found that the LORD had not abandoned him — the place of two camps, where the camp of God's people was joined by the unseen camp of God's host. The believer in his own fears may take the same comfort: those that be with us are more than those that be against us (2 Kings 6:16).

etymology: Hebrew Ramah (H7414), "height, high place" (from rum, "to be high"). Several towns bear the name; chiefly Ramah of Benjamin / Ephraim, the home of Samuel, and Ramah associated with Rachel's weeping.
biblical_def: Ramah ("height") was the name of several towns in Israel, the most significant being the Ramah that was the home, judgment-seat, and burial place of the prophet Samuel, and the Ramah associated in prophecy with Rachel weeping for her children. Samuel's Ramah (Ramathaim-zophim) was the town of his father Elkanah and his mother Hannah (1 Sam 1:1, 19); it was Samuel's home throughout his life, the seat from which he judged Israel on his yearly circuit (1 Sam 7:17), the place to which the elders of Israel came to demand a king (1 Sam 8:4), and the place of his death and burial, where all Israel mourned him (1 Sam 25:1). It was at Ramah, in the company of the prophets, that David fled to Samuel from Saul, and where the Spirit of God came mightily even upon Saul's messengers and upon Saul himself (1 Sam 19:18-24). The other great association of Ramah is prophetic and sorrowful: Jeremiah, foreseeing the exile, wrote, "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not" (Jer 31:15) — Ramah being near where the captives were gathered for deportation, and near Rachel's traditional burial place. The Gospel of Matthew applies this very verse to the slaughter of the innocents at Bethlehem by Herod, when the children were killed in the attempt to destroy the infant Christ (Matt 2:17-18). Ramah thus carries a double weight: the place of Samuel the great prophet and intercessor, and the place of the deepest maternal grief, taken up by the Spirit to describe both the sorrow of the exile and the sorrow of Bethlehem — grief that, in Jeremiah's own context, is immediately followed by the promise of the new covenant and the return (Jer 31:16-17, 31-34).

corruption_summary: Ramah is corrupted when its several locations are confused without care, when the Jeremiah 31:15 lament is severed from its context of new-covenant hope, or when Matthew's application of it to the slaughter of the innocents is misread as a strained proof-text rather than a Spirit-given connection.
corruption_paragraphs: Lament-severed-from-hope. Jeremiah 31:15, "a voice was heard in Ramah... Rachel weeping for her children," is one of the most sorrowful verses in Scripture, and it is sometimes quoted as a bare expression of grief. In Jeremiah its setting is crucial: the very next verses turn from weeping to hope — "Refrain thy voice from weeping... thy children shall come again" (Jer 31:16-17) — and the same chapter contains the great promise of the new covenant (Jer 31:31-34). The weeping of Ramah is real, but it is bounded by the promise of return and of the new covenant in Christ. The Spirit who recorded the lament recorded also the comfort.

Matthew's-application misread. Matthew applies Jeremiah's "voice in Ramah" to the weeping at Bethlehem when Herod slaughtered the infants in his attempt to kill the child Christ (Matt 2:17-18). Critics sometimes treat this as a strained or arbitrary proof-text. The connection is rich and deliberate: as Israel wept when the children were carried into exile, so the mothers of Bethlehem wept when the children were slain — and in both cases the weeping is taken up into the larger purpose of God, who brings His people back from exile and who preserves His Son through the slaughter to accomplish the redemption that turns weeping into joy. Matthew, writing by the same Spirit who inspired Jeremiah, draws the line the Spirit intended.

etymology: Hebrew Adullam (H5725), an ancient Canaanite town in the lowland (Shephelah) of Judah; the meaning is uncertain, possibly "refuge" or "justice of the people." Famous for the cave of Adullam, David's stronghold.
biblical_def: Adullam was an ancient town in the lowland of Judah, famous for the cave of Adullam, the stronghold to which David fled from Saul, and where the band of his mighty men first gathered to him. After David escaped from the Philistine city of Gath, "David therefore departed thence, and escaped to the cave Adullam: and when his brethren and all his father's house heard it, they went down thither to him. And every one that was in distress, and every one that was in debt, and every one that was discontented, gathered themselves unto him; and he became a captain over them: and there were with him about four hundred men" (1 Sam 22:1-2). The cave of Adullam is one of the great pictures of the Scriptures. To it came not the strong, the prosperous, and the content, but the distressed, the indebted, and the discontented — the desperate and the marginal of Israel, who gathered to the rejected, anointed-but-not-yet-enthroned king. Under David's leadership these outcasts were forged into the mighty men, the famous warriors of his kingdom (2 Sam 23). It was at Adullam that three of these mighty men broke through the Philistine garrison to bring David water from the well of Bethlehem, which he would not drink but poured out to the LORD (2 Sam 23:13-17). Adullam has long been read by the church as a type of Christ and His kingdom: to the rejected king, despised and outside the centers of power, gather the distressed, the debtors, and the discontented — sinners in need, who find in Him a captain and a refuge, and who are transformed under His leadership into a people of valor. As men gathered to David in the cave, so sinners gather to Christ; the King receives the desperate, and makes the outcast His mighty men.

corruption_summary: Adullam is corrupted only when the cave is read as bare military history rather than as the great picture of the kingdom it has always been to the church, or when the transformation of the outcasts into mighty men under David is overlooked.
corruption_paragraphs: Military-history reduction. The cave of Adullam can be read as a mere stage in David's guerrilla campaign against Saul. The Scriptures and the church have always seen more. The detail of who gathered to David — not the strong and content but the distressed, the indebted, the discontented — is theologically pointed. To the rejected, anointed-but-not-yet-crowned king came the desperate and the marginal, and he became their captain. The cave is the gospel in picture: Christ, the rejected King, receives not the self-sufficient but the needy, the burdened, the bankrupt sinner who has nowhere else to go (Matt 11:28). The desperate who gather to Him find a captain and a refuge.

Adullam has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal point worth recovering is its long-recognized typology of Christ and His kingdom. As the distressed, indebted, and discontented gathered to David at Adullam and were forged into mighty men, so spiritually-bankrupt sinners gather to the rejected King Jesus and are transformed by Him into a holy people. The King is not ashamed to call them brethren (Heb 2:11). What they were when they came — desperate, marginal, in debt — is not what they became under His leadership. Adullam preaches the gospel of the King who receives the needy and makes them mighty.

etymology: Hebrew Gibe'on (H1391), "hill city" (from geva, "hill"). A Canaanite city north of Jerusalem whose inhabitants deceived Israel into a treaty (Josh 9). Distinct from Gibeah (Saul's town).
biblical_def: Gibeon was a prominent Canaanite city whose inhabitants, by a famous deception, secured a covenant of peace with Israel, and which became the scene of one of the great miracles of the conquest and the site of the tabernacle in David's day. When the Israelites entered Canaan, the Gibeonites, hearing of the destruction of Jericho and Ai, feared for their lives. Rather than fight, they resorted to cunning: they sent ambassadors in worn-out clothes with moldy bread, pretending to be travelers from a far country, and persuaded Joshua and the elders to make a covenant with them (Josh 9). The text records Israel's failure: "the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD" (Josh 9:14). When the deception was discovered three days later, Israel honored the oath they had sworn rather than break covenant, but made the Gibeonites "hewers of wood and drawers of water" for the house of God (Josh 9:21-27). The episode teaches the danger of acting without seeking the LORD's counsel, and the binding seriousness of a sworn oath even when obtained by deceit (centuries later, Saul's violation of this oath by killing Gibeonites brought a famine in David's day, 2 Sam 21). When the kings of the southern Canaanites attacked Gibeon for making peace with Israel, Joshua came to its defense, and the LORD fought for Israel, casting down great hailstones and causing the sun to stand still over Gibeon for about a whole day — "there was no day like that before it or after it" (Josh 10:11-14). Later, the tabernacle and the bronze altar stood at the high place of Gibeon (1 Chr 16:39; 21:29), and there the LORD appeared to the young King Solomon in a dream and granted his request for wisdom (1 Kings 3:4-15). Gibeon thus combines a lesson in the danger of prayerlessness, a testimony to the binding nature of covenant oaths, the memory of the sun standing still, and the place where Solomon received wisdom from God.

corruption_summary: Gibeon is corrupted when the lesson of prayerless decision is missed, when the binding force of the oath is dismissed as legalism, or when the sun-standing-still miracle is explained away rather than received as the LORD's mighty act for His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Prayerless-decision lesson missed. The heart of the Gibeon deception is Israel's failure stated plainly: "the men took of their victuals, and asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD" (Josh 9:14). They judged by appearances — the worn clothes, the moldy bread — and did not seek the LORD, and so were deceived into a covenant they would not have made. The lesson is permanent and searching: God's people are led into error not chiefly by the cunning of others but by their own failure to seek the LORD's counsel before acting. The remedy for being deceived is prayer; the cause of much trouble is the prayerlessness that trusts its own discernment of appearances.

Oath-binding dismissed. When the deception was discovered, Israel did not break the covenant, though it had been obtained by lies; they honored their sworn oath, because the name of the LORD had been invoked in it (Josh 9:19-20). Modern readers may find this strange — why keep an oath secured by fraud? The Scripture treats the sworn oath, taken in the LORD's name, as binding even at cost (Ps 15:4, "he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not"), and the later famine that fell when Saul violated this very oath (2 Sam 21) shows how seriously God regards it. The episode rebukes a casual age that treats vows and oaths as disposable: a word sworn before God binds, and the LORD requires it to be kept.

etymology: Hebrew Qe'ilah (H7084), a fortified town in the lowland of Judah; the meaning is uncertain. Famous as the city David delivered, whose men would have betrayed him to Saul.
biblical_def: Keilah was a fortified town in the lowland of Judah that David delivered from the Philistines, and which became the scene of a striking episode in which David twice inquired of the LORD and learned that the very men he had saved would betray him. While David was a fugitive from Saul, word came that the Philistines were fighting against Keilah and robbing its threshing-floors. David inquired of the LORD whether he should go to its rescue; the LORD said go; his men, fearful, hesitated; David inquired again, was again told to go, and so he delivered Keilah, smiting the Philistines and saving its inhabitants (1 Sam 23:1-5). But when Saul heard that David was shut up within the walled town, he prepared to come and besiege it. David, learning of Saul's intent, inquired of the LORD through the ephod: "Will the men of Keilah deliver me up into his hand? ... Will the men of Keilah deliver up me and my men into the hand of Saul? And the LORD said, They will deliver thee up" (1 Sam 23:11-12). So David and his men departed from Keilah before Saul could trap him there. The episode is rich in instruction. It shows David's habit of inquiring of the LORD at every turn, twice before the rescue and again before the danger. It shows the LORD's gracious foreknowledge: God knew and told David what the men of Keilah WOULD do (deliver him up) under circumstances that, because David fled, never came to pass — a clear testimony to God's exhaustive knowledge of contingent events (against the Open-Theist denial of such foreknowledge). And it shows the sad truth that those whom we deliver may yet betray us: David saved Keilah at the risk of his life, and its men were ready to hand him to Saul to save themselves. The believer learns from Keilah to seek the LORD's guidance in everything, to rest in His perfect knowledge of all that is and all that would be, and not to be surprised when ingratitude repays kindness.

corruption_summary: Keilah is corrupted when David's repeated inquiry of the LORD is overlooked, when the LORD's foreknowledge of what the men WOULD do is explained away (as Open Theism must), or when the lesson about ingratitude is missed.
corruption_paragraphs: Foreknowledge-of-contingents missed. The Keilah episode is a clear and important testimony to God's exhaustive foreknowledge, including the foreknowledge of contingent events that never actually occur. The LORD told David that the men of Keilah WOULD deliver him up to Saul, and that Saul WOULD come down — yet because David acted on this knowledge and fled, neither event came to pass. God thus knew, and truly declared, what free agents would do under circumstances that did not materialize. This refutes the Open-Theist claim (the dictionary's open-theism entry) that God cannot know future free decisions: the God of Scripture knew not only what would happen but what would have happened, and acted to direct His servant by that knowledge. "Known unto God are all his works from the beginning" (Acts 15:18).

Keilah has no significant postmodern redefinition. The principal points worth recovering are David's habit of inquiring of the LORD before every step (twice before the rescue, again before the danger), and the searching lesson that those we deliver may yet betray us. David risked his life to save Keilah; its men were ready to hand him over to save themselves. The believer learns to seek God's guidance in all things (Prov 3:5-6), to rest in His perfect knowledge of all that is and would be, and not to be embittered when kindness is repaid with ingratitude, as it was for David and supremely for the Lord Jesus.

A testimony to God's foreknowledge of contingent events (against Open Theism) and to ingratitude repaying kindness
usage: Keilah — the town David delivered from the Philistines, whose men would have betrayed him to Saul.
The LORD told David the men of Keilah would deliver him up (1 Sam 23:12): God knows even what would have been.
David saved Keilah at the risk of his life; its men were ready to betray him — ingratitude repaying kindness.
